evidence.reference_title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Central Nervous System Infections in the Emergency Department.
evidence.snippet: Patients with CNS infection can present to the ED with nonspecific signs and symptoms, including headache, fever, altered mental status, and behavioral changes.

evidence.reference_title: Acute bacterial meningitis: current review and treatment update.
evidence.snippet: The classic triad of bacterial meningitis consists of fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status; headache is also another common symptom.

evidence.reference_title: Clinical Predictors of Malaria, Acute Bacterial Meningitis and Treatment Outcomes among Febrile Children Admitted with Altered Mental Status in Northwestern Tanzania.
evidence.snippet: BACKGROUND: Malaria and acute bacterial meningitis (ABM) are the leading infectious causes of febrile encephalopathy in malaria endemic settings. The clinical distinction of the two conditions is complicated by overlap in clinical features.

evidence.reference_title: Analysis of clinical outcomes in pediatric bacterial meningitis focusing on patients without cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis.
evidence.snippet: BACKGROUND: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cell count and biochemical examinations and cultures form the basis for the diagnosis of bacterial meningitis. However, some patients do not have typical findings and are at a higher risk of being missed or having delayed treatment.

evidence.reference_title: [Cognitive Impairment in Patients with Bacterial Meningitis and Encephalitides].
evidence.snippet: Cognitive impairments, including dementia, can present as first symptoms at the acute stage, and/or as sequelae in the chronic stages, in some patients with bacterial meningitis (BM) or encephalitides.

nodes.description: Bacteria enter the bloodstream and cross the blood-brain barrier to infect the meninges.

evidence.reference_title: How Does Streptococcus pneumoniae Invade the Brain?
evidence.snippet: Streptococcus pneumoniae (the pneumococcus) is the major cause of bacterial meningitis. The mechanisms by which pneumococci from the bloodstream penetrate the blood-brain barrier to reach the brain are not fully understood.

evidence.reference_title: Investigating Bacterial Penetration of the Blood-Brain Barrier for the Pathogenesis, Prevention, and Therapy of Bacterial Meningitis.
evidence.snippet: Microbial penetration of the blood-brain barrier, a prerequisite for the development of bacterial meningitis, exploits specific host and bacterial factors as well as host cell signaling molecules.

evidence.reference_title: Listeria monocytogenes meningitis in the elderly: epidemiological, clinical and therapeutic findings.
evidence.snippet: If the infection is not controlled at the stage in which the bacterium is in the liver, for instance, due to a severe immunodepression, a secondary bacteraemia can be developed and L. monocytogenes reaches the preferred sites transgressing the blood-brain barrier or the placental barrier.

evidence.reference_title: Bacterial penetration across the blood-brain barrier during the development of neonatal meningitis.
evidence.snippet: Transcellular penetration, e.g., transcytosis across the BBB has been demonstrated for Escherichia coli K1, group B streptococcus, Listeria monocytogenes, Citrobacter freundii and Streptococcus pneumonia strains.

nodes.description: Empiric meningitis therapy adds vancomycin to cover beta-lactam-resistant pneumococci. Vancomycin binds the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of the membrane lipid II peptidoglycan precursor, sequestering the substrate so cross-linking cannot proceed — a different step of the same cell-wall pathway than the cephalosporin target, which is why the two are combined empirically.

evidence.reference_title: Vancomycin derivative with damaged D-Ala-D-Ala binding cleft binds to cross-linked peptidoglycan in the cell wall of Staphylococcus aureus.
evidence.snippet: the antimicrobial activity of other vancosamine-modified glycopeptides depends upon both d-Ala-d-Ala stem-terminus recognition (primary binding site) and stem-bridge recognition (secondary binding site).

nodes.description: The major bacterial causes of meningitis (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae, group B Streptococcus, Listeria) build their peptidoglycan cell wall by penicillin-binding protein (PBP) transpeptidase cross-linking. This essential, bacteria-specific reaction is the target of the third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone/cefotaxime) backbone of empiric therapy; CNS-penetrant beta-lactams acylate the PBP active site, halt cross-linking, and are bactericidal in the CSF.

evidence.reference_title: From the regulation of peptidoglycan synthesis to bacterial growth and morphology.
evidence.snippet: although glycan chain polymerization occurs in the absence of transpeptidation (for example, in the presence of penicillin), efficient transpeptidation requires ongoing GTase reactions

nodes.description: Broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone, vancomycin) started immediately after lumbar puncture.

evidence.reference_title: Role of empiric parenteral antibiotics prior to lumbar puncture in suspected bacterial meningitis: state of the art.
evidence.snippet: The available evidence suggests that if bacterial meningitis is suspected and LP must be delayed, intravenous antibiotics are warranted before CSF is obtained.

evidence.reference_title: Vancomycin Should Be Part of Empiric Therapy for Suspected Bacterial Meningitis.
evidence.snippet: The use of empiric vancomycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin for suspected bacterial meningitis has been recommended since 1997.

evidence.reference_title: Bacterial meningitis.
evidence.snippet: Empiric antimicrobial and adjunctive therapy should be initiated as soon as a single set of blood cultures has been obtained.

evidence.reference_title: Empiric Antibiotics for Serious Bacterial Infection in Young Infants: Opportunities for Stewardship.
evidence.snippet: Empiric therapy was ampicillin and gentamicin (n = 116, 44%) or third-generation cephalosporin based (n = 149, 56%).

evidence.reference_title: Progress and Challenges in Bacterial Meningitis: A Review.
evidence.snippet: Up to 24% of those who survive develop chronic neurological sequelae, such as hearing loss or focal neurological deficits.

evidence.reference_title: Progress and Challenges in Bacterial Meningitis: A Review.
evidence.snippet: Brain imaging should be performed before lumbar puncture if patients present with altered mental status, focal neurological deficits, papilledema, or history of immunocompromising conditions or central nervous system disease.

nodes.description: Inflammation and accumulation of purulent exudate lead to increased intracranial pressure.

evidence.reference_title: Brain edema and increased intracranial pressure in the pathophysiology of bacterial meningitis.
evidence.snippet: Their presence in the cerebrospinal fluid is associated with the induction of inflammation and with the development of brain edema and increased intracranial pressure.

evidence.reference_title: Fulminant bacterial meningitis.
evidence.snippet: Fulminant bacterial meningitis is a rare host reaction to infection characterized by sudden onset, rapid deterioration, abrupt cerebral edema and refractory intracranial hypertension.

evidence.reference_title: Bacterial Infections of the Central Nervous System.
evidence.snippet: Acute bacterial meningitis may present with symptoms as nonspecific as headache and fever, but rapid progression to an altered level of consciousness is not unusual.

evidence.reference_title: Excess glutamate levels in the cerebrospinal fluid predict clinical outcome of bacterial meningitis.
evidence.snippet: The clinical course of bacterial meningitis still is characterized by a high mortality and frequent neurological deficits in survivors.

evidence.reference_title: Management of bacterial menigitis in 2016.
evidence.snippet: Seizures should be avoided, the sedation-pain control optimized and ventilation adapted to assure normal oxygenation and normal CO₂ levels.

evidence.reference_title: Bacterial Infections of the Central Nervous System.
evidence.snippet: Brain abscess may initially present only with headache, or as a new-onset seizure or with a focal neurological deficit.

nodes.description: Active immunization with polysaccharide-protein conjugate vaccines against Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), Streptococcus pneumoniae (PCV), and Neisseria meningitidis serogroups A, C, W, and Y (MenACWY) — together with outer-membrane protein vaccines against N. meningitidis serogroup B (MenB) — induces opsonophagocytic and bactericidal anticapsular or anti-surface-protein antibodies that reduce nasopharyngeal carriage, clear bloodstream bacteremia, and prevent bacterial invasion of the meninges.

evidence.reference_title: Vaccines against bacterial meningitis.
evidence.snippet: Effective routine immunization against Hib, pneumococcus and serogroupC meningococcus has had a significant impact on both invasive disease and carriage caused by these encapsulated bacteria.

evidence.reference_title: Hib Vaccines: Past, Present, and Future Perspectives.
evidence.snippet: The Hib conjugate vaccine is considered protective and safe.

evidence.reference_title: Prophylaxis of bacterial meningitis.
evidence.snippet: A comprehensive review of all major agents causing bacterial meningitis--meningococcus of the groups A, B, C, W135, and Y, pneumococcus, and Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib)--is done in terms of preventing them by chemoprophylaxis or vaccination.

evidence.reference_title: Global status of Haemophilus influenzae type b and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines: evidence, policies, and introductions.
evidence.snippet: The leading causes of bacterial meningitis and pneumonia in children, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) and Streptococcus pneumoniae, are vaccine preventable.

evidence.reference_title: Meningococcal vaccine: a new vaccine to combat meningococcal disease in India.
evidence.snippet: The meningococcal conjugate vaccines (MCV) are preferred for reasons of immunogenicity and persistence of immunity.
